A1.justification: Both PDFs describe SIMSplat, and their main text, equations, tables, and figures are readable. Neither contains an appendix or embedded supplement. v2 refers to supplementary implementation details, evaluation settings, and plausibility rubrics that are not supplied, limiting comparison of those details.

before.justification: v1 reports original Waymo experiments on object querying, editing-task completion, and motion failures in Tables 1–3, with qualitative editing results.

after.justification: v2 reports original Waymo experiments, including revised querying and editing results, language-feature ablations, and VLM-driven scenario-mining comparisons in Tables 2–6.

M1.justification: v2 Section 2.2 replaces bounding-box-prompted SAM-2 masks with masks obtained by projecting scene-graph Gaussian nodes. Section 2.3 adds a VLM loop for generating prompts, checking feasibility, evaluating rendered outputs, and iteratively adjusting assets or motion parameters. v1 describes human-directed LLM editing instead. Its final diffusion-inpainting stage is also absent from v2's described pipeline.

E1.justification: Both versions use Waymo driving scenes with vehicles, pedestrians, and static objects. v2 extends the evaluated task coverage to autonomous scenario generation from multi-view images and demonstrates aggressive cut-in and abrupt-reversing scenarios in Figure 5(b). No additional dataset or domain is reported.

E2.justification: The original external comparator roster is retained. v2 Table 6 adds within-pipeline comparisons among Qwen3-VL-32B, Qwen3-VL-8B, GPT-5, GPT-5-mini, and Claude-Opus-4.1. OmniRe is now explicitly marked as extended with editing functions, although the PDFs do not establish when that extension was implemented. HUGSIM appears in a capability checklist, not a reported performance experiment.

E3.justification: v2 adds evaluation of fully automated editing, comparing VLM configurations through iteration counts, task completion, and Gemini-assessed plausibility on a 1–4 scale. The existing camera selection, frame sampling, holdout rule, and motion-prediction horizon remain stated consistently. Evaluation sets and detailed protocols behind the revised legacy scores cannot be matched reliably from the supplied PDFs.

E4.justification: v2 Table 3 introduces controlled appearance-only, appearance-plus-motion, appearance-plus-location, and full-feature ablations, directly testing the alignment components. Table 6 additionally analyzes dependence on the VLM controller. The existing comparison with and without multi-agent refinement is retained.

E5.justification: Neither supplied PDF reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests. v2's editing-iteration counts measure convergence of the automated loop, not repeated experimental runs or statistical uncertainty.

E6.justification: All three original quantitative comparisons receive revised results. Reported SIMSplat overall querying accuracy/vIoU changes from 0.64/0.19 to 0.73/0.80; task completion changes from 84.2% to 87.2% for human-guided editing, with 71.1% newly reported for automation; motion failure changes from 10.4% to 20.0%. Baseline scores also change, and ablation/VLM results are added. These are changed reported outcomes, not established same-setting gains or losses.

T1.justification: The Gaussian compositing and scene-graph definitions, appearance encoding, trajectory codebooks, alignment objective, and motion-prediction expression are substantively retained. Equation numbering, notation, and explanatory wording change, but neither supplied PDF adds a theorem, proof, or substantive mathematical derivation.

C1.justification: v2 adds automated scenario mining as a fourth principal contribution and claims generation, validation, and refinement without manual intervention. Its abstract, introduction, and conclusion center on a unified language-accessible scene representation enabling this automation. The earlier grounding, pedestrian-editing, and multi-agent-refinement contributions remain.

C2.justification: v2 adds interpretations linking motion and location features to complementary grounding benefits and discusses VLM quality, iteration efficiency, and computational-cost tradeoffs. It removes v1 Table 1's explanation that ambiguous ground-truth masks depress vIoU. The limitation concerning prediction uncertainty and the option to bypass refinement remain.

D1.justification: v2 identifies Qwen3-VL-32B as the automation model and Gemini as the plausibility evaluator. However, v1's explicit OpenCLIP ViT-B/16 and E5-mistral-7B specifications and project-page link are absent from the supplied v2. Hardware and basic sampling details remain; further implementation settings and evaluation rubrics are deferred to unavailable supplementary material.

R1.justification: v1's dedicated related-work discussion is replaced by a shorter introduction-based positioning and a capability comparison table emphasizing unified grounding, editing, refinement, and automation. Discussion and citations concerning methods such as DGD and 4-LEGS disappear, while HUGSIM, Qwen3-VL, and work supporting VLM-based evaluation are added. This substantially changes research positioning beyond reference renumbering.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction, contribution list, and conclusion are extensively rewritten. The standalone Related Work section disappears, the LLM Agent subsection becomes Automated Scenario Mining, and Temporal Alignment becomes Motion-Aware Alignment. These constitute substantial narrative and organizational changes.

P2.justification: The paper changes from a two-column to a single-column layout. The editing-process diagram is redrawn around VLM generation and validation, the alignment diagram changes its mask-generation block, and Figure 5 is reorganized into human-guided and VLM-driven examples. New capability, feature-ablation, and VLM-comparison tables substantially expand the visual presentation.

improvement.justification: v2 Table 3 directly tests alignment components that v1 only motivated, strengthening evidence for a central contribution. The automated workflow also receives explicit evaluation in Tables 4 and 6. These benefits are tempered by unavailable supplementary protocols and rubrics and the omission of previously specified encoder models. The revised headline scores cannot establish comparable-setting performance improvements, so the supported overall quality gain is limited.
